documents.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Contrastive Re-ranking for Long-Form Question Answering
documents.content:
# Abstract

We present a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline developed at Google DeepMind that combines dense passage retrieval with contrastive re-ranking for long-form question answering. Our method improves ROUGE-L by 3.2 points over the strongest open baseline on the ELI5 and ASQA benchmarks while reducing inference cost by twelve percent. The contributions are a lightweight cross-encoder re-ranker trained with in-batch negatives drawn from the retriever's own top-k, and a hybrid scoring rule that interpolates lexical and semantic signals at query time.

# Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation has become the dominant approach for knowledge-grounded question answering. The pattern is familiar: a retriever surfaces candidate passages from a corpus, and a generator conditions on those passages to produce an answer. Quality is bounded above by the retriever — no amount of decoder capacity recovers a document the retriever missed. Our work targets the precision of the retrieved set rather than its recall.

# Methods

We trained a six-layer cross-encoder on 1.2 million (query, passage, label) triples mined from the retriever's own top-twenty candidates. Negatives came from within the same batch; the positive was the labeled gold passage. Training ran for three epochs on a single TPU v5e pod. At inference time, the retriever returns the top fifty candidates and the re-ranker scores all fifty in a single forward pass.

# Results

On ELI5 we report ROUGE-L of 24.8 against a best-prior baseline of 21.6. On ASQA we report 31.4 against a prior 28.1. Ablations confirm that in-batch negatives drawn from the retriever's own top-k contribute roughly two of the three points of improvement; the remainder comes from the hybrid lexical-semantic interpolation.

documents.title: Sparse Attention Revisited: Subquadratic Long-Context Transformers for Code and Prose
documents.content:
# Abstract

We at Meta AI revisit sparse attention patterns for long-context transformers and show that a simple strided-plus-local mask matches the perplexity of full attention up to 32k tokens while running thirty-one percent faster on an A100. The gains hold on both natural-language and source-code corpora. We release pretrained checkpoints and benchmark code.

# Introduction

Quadratic attention is the single biggest barrier to long-context transformers. Prior work has explored linear-attention approximations, recurrent compression, and hash-based routing, each with its own accuracy cliff. Our starting observation is that for most corpora the attention matrix is already sparse in practice — the model learns to attend locally with a few long-range spikes — so a hand-designed sparse pattern should not cost much perplexity if chosen carefully.

# Methods

The mask combines a sliding local window of 256 tokens with a strided global pattern at stride 512. Every query token attends to its local window and to one in every 512 tokens globally. We trained 1.3B-parameter decoder-only models from scratch on a 400B-token mixture for 80k steps. Evaluation used perplexity on held-out prose and exact-match on HumanEval-style code completion.

# Results

On a 32k-token prose benchmark we match dense attention within 0.15 perplexity points. On HumanEval-Plus we match within 0.8 percent pass@1. Wall-clock training speedup is 1.31x on an A100 40GB at sequence length 32k; the speedup grows to 1.9x at 64k, at which point dense attention runs out of memory.

documents.title: Graph Neural Networks for Molecular Property Prediction under Distribution Shift
documents.content:
# Abstract

Molecular property prediction models often degrade sharply when evaluated on scaffolds unseen during training. We at Stanford University introduce a domain-regularized graph neural network that narrows the in-domain-to-out-of-domain gap by 41% on MoleculeNet while matching in-domain performance. The regularizer is a cheap consistency loss between two forward passes under different edge-dropout masks.

# Introduction

Drug discovery is a scaffold-generalization problem. A model trained on one family of chemistries is asked to score candidates from an unseen family; benchmark numbers that do not split by scaffold overstate the real-world performance by a large margin. We propose a regularizer motivated by recent work on invariant risk minimization.

# Methods

During training, each molecule passes through the GNN twice with independently sampled edge-dropout masks at a rate of 0.15. We add a KL-divergence term between the two output distributions, weighted at 0.1. Backbone is a six-layer message-passing network with 256-dimensional node embeddings. We trained on the scaffold split of MoleculeNet for 100 epochs.

# Results

Averaged across BBBP, Tox21, and HIV datasets we report an AUROC gap between in-domain and scaffold-held-out splits of 0.061, versus a baseline gap of 0.104. In-domain AUROC is preserved within one standard deviation. Ablations show that dropout rate and KL weight both matter — either too high or too low collapses the benefit.
